ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint is a highly mobile ball‑and‑socket articulation that relies on muscular and capsular support. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose instability, rotator cuff tears, and infection, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The shoulder joint connects the humeral head to the glenoid fossa of the scapula, allowing the widest range of motion of any joint.
b: Ball‑and‑socket type
Most mobile joint in the body
Relies on soft‑tissue stabilisers

sections.p: The joint lies laterally on the upper thorax, deep to the deltoid, and is surrounded by the joint capsule, glenoid labrum, and rotator cuff tendons.
b: Glenoid cavity is shallow; labrum deepens it
Capsule reinforced by coracohumeral and glenohumeral ligaments
Rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis

sections.p: Anteriorly the joint is adjacent to the subscapularis and the axillary nerve; posteriorly it contacts the infraspinatus and teres minor; superiorly the acromion and clavicle form the AC joint.
b: Acromioclavicular joint lies superior
Bursa between deltoid and capsule reduces friction

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the joint via the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, branches of the axillary artery.
b: Anterior circumflex supplies the anterior capsule
Posterior circumflex supplies the posterior capsule and rotator cuff

sections.p: Sensory innervation comes from the suprascapular, axillary, and lateral pectoral nerves; motor supply to the rotator cuff is from the suprascapular and subscapular nerves.
b: Axillary nerve: lateral shoulder skin and deltoid
Suprascapular nerve: supraspinatus & infraspinatus

sections.p: Provides flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, internal and external rotation, and circumduction, essential for reaching and lifting.
b: Stability from rotator cuff and labrum
Mobility from shallow glenoid

sections.p: Instability, rotator cuff tears, adhesive capsulitis, and septic arthritis are common. In low‑resource settings, TB or bacterial infection may involve the joint.
b: Dislocation: usually anterior; assess neurovascular status
Rotator cuff tear: pain on abduction, weakness in external rotation
Septic arthritis: fever, severe pain, limited motion; consider TB in endemic areas

t.b: Detects dislocation, fractures, joint space narrowing; if unavailable, use clinical exam and ultrasound
Identifies rotator cuff tears and effusion; portable in low‑resource settings
Confirms septic arthritis; if culture unavailable, treat empirically for Staph aureus and consider TB PCR

sections.p: Key points to remember for bedside assessment and exams.
b: Apprehension test assesses anterior instability
Drop arm test screens supraspinatus tear
Passive external rotation limited in adhesive capsulitis

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive shoulder pain with fever (possible septic arthritis)
Severe deformity after trauma (possible dislocation or fracture)
Sudden loss of shoulder function with neurovascular deficits

faq.q: Why is the shoulder more prone to dislocation than other joints?
faq.a: The glenoid is shallow, giving the humeral head great freedom but less bony stability.

faq.q: What distinguishes adhesive capsulitis from rotator cuff tear?
faq.a: Adhesive capsulitis limits both active and passive motion; rotator cuff tear spares passive range.

faq.q: Can TB affect the shoulder joint?
faq.a: Yes, especially in endemic regions; presents with chronic pain, swelling, and systemic symptoms.

exam: Describe the bony and soft‑tissue structures that stabilise the glenohumeral joint.
Explain how you would differentiate an anterior shoulder dislocation from a rotator cuff tear on examination.
List the first‑line investigations for suspected septic arthritis of the shoulder and their diagnostic purpose.
